F1.quote: The PPS website screens the scientific literature for papers (partly) generated with: … Tortured phrases … SCIgen … Mathgen
F1.claim: what it is, by its own page: a website screening the literature for papers (partly) generated with tortured phrases, SCIgen and Mathgen
F1.lineage: what it is: a screener of the literature

F2.quote: ... and issues in the bibliographies of articles citing: … Retracted references … References marked with expressions of concern … References flagged by the PPS detectors
F2.claim: and screens bibliographies citing retracted references, references under expressions of concern, and references the PPS detectors flag
F2.lineage: the bibliographic detectors: Feet of Clay

F3.quote: Harvesting data from these APIs: … Crossref, now including the Retraction Watch Database … Dimensions, see our webinar and the associated blog post … PubMed … PubPeer
F3.claim: its data harvested from the APIs of Crossref (with the Retraction Watch Database), Dimensions, PubMed and PubPeer

F5.quote: Problematic papers are reported on PubPeer, see the tortured phrases and more.
F5.claim: problematic papers are reported on PubPeer

F6.quote: Detectors: … Annulled … Concerning … Feet of Clay … Tortured … Suspect … SCIgen … Mathgen … Citejacked … Seek&Blastn … Problematic Cell Lines
F6.claim: ten detectors listed: Annulled, Concerning, Feet of Clay, Tortured, Suspect, SCIgen, Mathgen, Citejacked, Seek&Blastn, Problematic Cell Lines

F7.quote: Cabanac, G., Labbé, C., & Magazinov, A. (2022). The ‘Problematic Paper Screener’ automatically selects suspect publications for post-publication (re)assessment. … Presented at WCRI 2022: 7th World Conference on Research Integrity.
F7.claim: the reference for the screener: Cabanac, Labbé and Magazinov (2022), presented at WCRI 2022

F8.quote: Featured in the Nature's 10 list of 2021 that ‘explores key developments in science this year.’

F10.locus: Key highlights, embedded post by Nature (8 August 2021)
F10.quote: Why say 'colossal information' instead of big data? Or 'counterfeit consciousness' instead of artificial intelligence? These tortured phases in research articles could be evidence of a new and disturbing fabrication trend.
F10.claim: Nature's examples of tortured phrases, quoted on the page: 'colossal information' for big data, 'counterfeit consciousness' for artificial intelligence; possible evidence of a fabrication trend

F11.quote: The Problematic Paper Screener trawls through 130 million scholarly papers every week looking for telltale signs that papers were produced by paper mills.
F11.claim: it trawls 130 million scholarly papers every week for signs of paper-mill production
F11.lineage: scale and cadence: 130 million a week

F12.quote: These nonsensical, and sometimes amusing, word sequences are among thousands of “tortured phrases” that sleuths have found littered throughout reputable scientific journals. … They typically result from using paraphrasing tools to evade plagiarism-detection software when stealing someone else’s text.
F12.claim: tortured phrases: nonsensical word sequences found in reputable journals, typically from paraphrasing tools used to evade plagiarism detection

F13.quote: Have you ever heard of the Joined Together States? … The phrases above are real examples of bungled synonyms for the United States, breast cancer, kidney failure, artificial neural networks, and lactose intolerance, respectively.
F13.claim: examples: 'Joined Together States' for the United States, and others

F14.quote: We are a pair of computer scientists at Université de Toulouse and Université Grenoble Alpes, both in France, who specialize in detecting bogus publications.
F14.claim: the authors: two computer scientists at Toulouse and Grenoble Alpes who specialize in detecting bogus publications

F15.quote: One of us, Guillaume Cabanac, has built an automated tool that combs through 130 million scientific publications every week and flags those containing tortured phrases.
F15.claim: Cabanac built the automated tool, which combs 130 million publications a week and flags tortured phrases

F16.quote: The Problematic Paper Screener also includes eight other detectors, each of which looks for a specific type of problematic content.
F16.claim: eight other detectors besides tortured phrases, each for one type of problematic content

F17.quote: In addition to tortured phrases, the Problematic Paper Screener flags ChatGPT fingerprints: snippets of telltale text left behind by the AI agent.
F17.claim: it flags ChatGPT fingerprints, telltale text left by the AI agent

F18.quote: Several publishers use our paper screener, which has been instrumental in more than 1,000 retractions. Some have integrated the technology into the editorial workflow to spot suspect papers upfront.
F18.claim: several publishers use it; instrumental in more than 1,000 retractions; some integrate it into the editorial workflow

F19.quote: Analytics companies have used the screener for things like picking out suspect authors from lists of highly cited researchers.
F19.claim: analytics companies have used it to pick out suspect authors among highly cited researchers

F20.quote: It was named one of 10 key developments in science by the journal Nature in 2021.
F20.claim: named one of Nature's 10 key developments of 2021 (the article's wording)

F21.quote: Nearly 19,000 papers containing at least five tortured phrases each.
F21.claim: nearly 19,000 papers with at least five tortured phrases each

F22.quote: More than 280 gibberish papers – some still in circulation – written entirely by the spoof SCIgen program that Massachusetts Institute of Technology students came up with nearly 20 years ago.
F22.claim: more than 280 SCIgen papers, some still in circulation

F23.quote: More than 764,000 articles that cite retracted works that could be unreliable. About 5,000 of these articles have at least five retracted references listed in their bibliographies. We called the software that finds these the “Feet of Clay” detector
F23.claim: more than 764,000 articles cite retracted works (about 5,000 with five or more); the detector that finds them is Feet of Clay

F24.quote: More than 70 papers containing ChatGPT “fingerprints” with obvious signs such as “Regenerate Response” or “As an AI language model, I cannot …” in the text.
F24.claim: more than 70 papers with ChatGPT fingerprints

F25.quote: These articles represent the tip of the tip of the iceberg: They are cases where ChatGPT output has been copy-pasted wholesale into papers without any editing (or even reading) and has also slipped past peer reviewers and journal editors alike.
F25.claim: its limit: the fingerprinted papers are the tip of the tip of the iceberg, output copy-pasted wholesale

F26.quote: The challenge is to identify cases where chatbots are used not just for language-editing purposes but to generate content – essentially fabricating data.
F26.claim: the open challenge: chatbots used to generate content, not only to edit language

F27.quote: He is the administrator of the Problematic Paper Screener, a public platform that uses metadata from Digital Science and PubPeer via no-cost agreements.
F27.claim: Cabanac administers it, a public platform using Digital Science and PubPeer metadata under no-cost agreements

F28.quote: Cabanac has been in touch with most of the major publishers and their integrity officers, offering pro bono consulting regarding detection tools to various actors in the field including ClearSkies, Morressier, River Valley, Signals, and STM.
F28.claim: pro bono consulting on detection tools to publishers and actors including ClearSkies, Morressier, River Valley, Signals and STM

F29.quote: Post publication assessment remains necessary to check erroneous or fraudulent scientific publications.
F29.claim: the problem: post-publication assessment remains necessary for erroneous or fraudulent publications

F30.quote: We present an online platform, the 'Problematic Paper Screener' (this https URL) that leverages both automatic machine detection and human assessment to identify and flag already published problematic articles.
F30.claim: an online platform combining automatic machine detection and human assessment to identify and flag published problematic articles
F30.lineage: what it is: a screener of the literature

F31.quote: We provide a new effective tool to curate the scientific literature.
F31.claim: a new effective tool to curate the scientific literature

F32.quote: Authors:Guillaume Cabanac, Cyril Labbé, Alexander Magazinov … [Submitted on 7 Oct 2022] … Presented at WCRI 2022: 7th World Conference on Research Integrity, Cape Town, South Africa. 29 May -- 1 June 2022
F32.claim: authors Cabanac, Labbé, Magazinov; submitted 7 October 2022; presented at WCRI 2022, Cape Town

F33.quote: The Problematic Paper Screener, an academic project led by Guillaume Cabanac and collaborators, combines automatic machine detection and human evaluation to identify issues in publications, including the presence of tortured phrases.
F33.claim: an academic project led by Cabanac and collaborators, combining machine detection and human evaluation
F33.lineage: method: machine detection with human assessment

F34.quote: We’re excited to announce the integration of articles flagged by the Problematic Paper Screener into the Signals Graph as a new signal. This includes over 12,000 problematic publications that have not been retracted. These problematic publications are cited more than 160,000 times by articles.
F34.claim: flagged articles integrated into the Signals Graph: over 12,000 unretracted problematic publications, cited more than 160,000 times

F35.quote: We aim to help sleuths, publishers, and researchers gain greater visibility of these problematic papers and enable them to uncover additional research integrity issues with Signals.
F35.claim: Signals' aim: visibility of the problematic papers for sleuths, publishers and researchers

F36.quote: The PPS is a tool designed to identify and filter out potentially problematic scientific articles, such as those containing methodological errors, plagiarism, data manipulation, or conflicts of interest.
F36.claim: an adopter's description: a tool to identify and filter out problematic articles (methodological errors, plagiarism, data manipulation, conflicts of interest)

F37.quote: Developed by G. Cabanac, C. Labbé, and A. Magazinov , it provides a database of over one million references identified as containing problematic elements, categorised according to a typology that distinguishes between anomalies of varying severity – ranging from articles written entirely by AI to articles that are valid but contain references with anomalies (“Feet of clay”).
F37.claim: a database of over one million problematic references, typed by severity from AI-written articles to valid articles with anomalous references (Feet of clay)

F38.quote: This database is now available among the Episciences tools. It is used to analyze citations extracted from articles, detect and then display problematic citations, either for correction or for informational purposes.
F38.claim: Episciences uses the database to analyse extracted citations and display problematic ones

F39.locus: Toward a more comprehensive and automated verification solution ¶2
F39.quote: The platform takes this process a step further by incorporating automatic reference verification right after the submission is received, to help assess its quality, and subsequently by automatically updating any references that are retracted or change status after publication. This automatic check is performed using the PPS database.
F39.claim: Episciences' automatic reference check, at submission and after publication, runs on the PPS database

F40.quote: the first step involved analyzing nearly 170,000 references from an initial data extraction. The results of this analysis identified 226 references indexed in the PPS, the majority of which fall into the “Feet of clay” category.
F40.claim: of nearly 170,000 references analysed, 226 indexed in the PPS, most in Feet of clay

F41.claim: a Crossref webinar on Retraction Watch data in Crossref, 9 May 2025
